blocks.title: Stoichiometry
blocks.text: Stoichiometry is a branch of chemistry which tells us the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation.

With the knowledge of mole, Avogadro’s number, molar mass, molar volume, and molar concentration, we can establish quantitative relationships between reactants and products using the balanced chemical equations.
The following types of relationship can be studied with the help of a balanced chemical equation involving quantities of reactant(s) and product(s).
To understand these relationships, we need to interpret information hidden in a balanced chemical equation which is used to make stoichiometric calculations. For example:
This equation can be described in three different ways;

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says “three different ways” but lists four (moles, molecules, volumes and masses).

items: 1 mole of N₂ reacts with 3 moles of H₂ to form 2 moles of NH₃.
1 molecule of N₂ reacts with 3 molecules of H₂ to form 2 molecules of NH₃.
22.4 dm³ of N₂ reacts with 67.2 dm³ of H₂ to form 44.8 dm³ of NH₃
28.0 g of N₂ react with 6 g of H₂ to form 34.0 g of NH₃.

blocks.title: Keep in Mind!
blocks.text:
The following assumptions must be made while performing stoichiometric calculations:
1) All the reactants are completely converted into the products.
2) Law of conservation of mass and law of definite proportions are obeyed.
3) No side reaction occurs.

blocks.alt: Five rounded boxes stacked vertically and joined by downward arrows: yellow (mass of known solid, volume of known gas or molar concentration of known solution), green (calculate moles of the known using the relevant formula), red (ratio of known and unknown from the balanced equation), blue (moles of the unknown using the relevant formula) and orange (convert moles of the unknown to mass, volume or concentration).
blocks.caption: Approach to do stoichiometric calculations (original drawing after the scheme printed on p82 of the textbook).
blocks.long_description: Box 1: Mass of known solid or volume of a known gas, or molar concentration of known solution. Box 2: Calculate number of moles of known solid or volume of a known gas, or molar concentration of known solution using the relevant formula. Box 3: Find the ratio of the known and the unknown reactant or product from the balanced chemical equation. Box 4: Calculate the number of moles of the unknown reactant or product using the relevant formula. Box 5: Convert the number of moles of the unknown to mass, volume, or concentration of the substance.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed third box reads “unknow”; the word is unknown.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.11 (Mole-Mole Conversion)
blocks.problem: When 3.3 mole of nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to form ammonia, how many moles of hydrogen are consumed in the process? The equation for this reaction is N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
steps: Number of moles of N₂ = 3.3 mol
Number of moles of H₂ = ?
1 mole of N₂ needs H₂ to produce NH₃ = 3/1 = 3mol
blocks.answer: 3.6 moles of N₂ needs H₂ to produce NH₃ = 3 × 3.3 = 9.9 mol

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question gives 3.3 mol of N₂, not 3.6 moles; 3.3 mol of N₂ needs 3 × 3.3 = 9.9 mol of H₂, as calculated.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.12 (Mass-Mass Conversion)
blocks.problem: Calculate the mass of Al needed to react completely with 32.0 g of iron (III) oxide according to the equation given below: 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s).
steps: Molar mass of Fe₂O₃, M = 159.6 g mol⁻¹
Number of moles of Fe₂O₃ (n) = m/M = 32.0 g / 159.6 g mol⁻¹ = 0.02 mol
From the balanced equation, 1 mol of Fe₂O₃ reacts with 2 moles of Al, therefore, number of moles of Al that reacts with 0.02 mole of Fe₂O₃ = 2 x 0.02 = 0.04 mol
Mass of Al = n x M = 0.04 mol x 27 g mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 32.0 / 159.6 = 0.200 mol of Fe₂O₃, not 0.02 mol. So Al = 2 × 0.200 = 0.401 mol, and the mass of Al = 0.401 mol × 27 g mol⁻¹ = 10.8 g, not 1.08 g.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.13 (Volume-Volume)
blocks.problem: Calculate volume of ammonia that can be produced by the reaction of 100 dm³ of hydrogen with excess of nitrogen at STP? The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
steps: Volume of hydrogen = 100 dm³
Volume of ammonia = ?
67.2 dm³ (3 mol) of H₂ produce ammonia = 44.8 dm³ (2 mol)
1 dm³ of H₂ produce ammonia = 44.8/67.2 = 2/3
100 dm³ of H₂ produce ammonia = 2/3 x 100 = 66.7 dm³
blocks.answer: So, the volume of ammonia produced by the reaction of 100 dm³ of H₂ with excess nitrogen is 66.7 dm³.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.14 Mole-Mass calculations
blocks.problem: Solid lithium hydroxide LiOH is used in space vehicles. It is employed to remove exhaled carbon dioxide from the living environment by forming solid lithium carbonate and liquid water. Calculate the mass of Li₂CO₃ that can be produced by 20.0 mol of LiOH. 2LiOH(s) + CO₂(g) → Li₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l)
steps: According to the given balanced chemical equation,
2 moles of LiOH produces = 1 mole Li₂CO₃
20.0 moles of LiOH produces = 1/2 × 20.0 = 10.0 mol Li₂CO₃
Mass of Li₂CO₃ produced = No. of mole × Molar mass
Mass of Li₂CO₃ produced = 10.0 mol × 73.9 g mol⁻¹ = 739.0 g
blocks.answer: Thus, 739.0 g Li₂CO₃ will be produced from 20.0 moles of LiOH.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.15 (Mass-mole calculations)
blocks.problem: Baking soda (NaHCO₃) acts as an antacid. It can neutralize excess hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted by the stomach according to equation. NaHCO₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(aq) How many moles of HCl will be neutralized by 2.1 g of baking soda
steps: Molar mass of NaHCO₃ = 84.0 g mol⁻¹
Moles of NaHCO₃ = 2.1 g / 84.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.025 mol
Stoichiometrically, the mole ratio of HCl and NaHCO₃ is 1 : 1.
Hence moles of HCl used = 0.025 mol
blocks.answer: Thus 2.1 g of NaHCO₃ will neutralize 0.025 moles of HCl.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Baking soda is a solid, not a gas: the reactant is NaHCO₃(s), not NaHCO₃(g). NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.16 (Mass-Volume Conversion)
blocks.problem: What volume of hydrogen at STP will be produced when 7.0 g of iron are reacted with an excess of sulphuric acid? Fe(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
steps: Molar mass of Fe (M) = 55.8 g/mol
Number of moles of iron (n) = m/M = 7.0 g / 55.8 gmol⁻¹ = 0.125 mol
From the balanced equation, 1 mol of iron produces 1 mole of hydrogen.
So, number of moles of H₂ = 0.125 mol
Volume of H₂ in dm³ = molar volume x moles of H₂ = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ x 0.125 mol
